title: Measure Exactly With Two Jugs
statement:
You have two unmarked jugs that hold a and b litres, an unlimited tap and a drain. Both jugs start empty. One move is any of these:

  • fill one jug to the top from the tap,
  • pour one jug out completely,
  • pour one jug into the other until the first is empty or the second is full, whichever comes first.

Return true if, after some number of moves, the two jugs together hold exactly target litres. Otherwise return false.

examples.why: Fill the 6, pour it into the 4 (2 left), empty the 4, pour the 2 across, fill the 6 again: 2 + 6 = 8.
Every move keeps both amounts even, so an odd total can never appear, even though 5 fits in the jugs.
Both jugs together hold only 8 litres.

hints: Try a few small jug pairs by hand. Which totals can you reach with a 4 and a 6? Notice what they all have in common.
Find something every move preserves. If both jugs hold a multiple of some number d, and d divides a and b, does any move break that?
The amounts x·a + y·b over all integers x, y are exactly the multiples of gcd(a, b) (Bézout). Combine that with the fact that the jugs cannot hold more than a + b.

explain.intuition:
Let g = gcd(a, b). At the start both jugs hold 0, a multiple of g. Filling sets a jug to a or b, emptying sets it to 0, and pouring moves min(x, room left), a difference of multiples of g. So every move keeps both amounts multiples of g, and so the total too.

The reverse is also true: every multiple of g between 0 and a + b can be reached. The classic routine of "fill the small jug, pour into the big one, empty the big one when it is full" walks through the multiples of g one by one. So the answer is just two checks: target ≤ a + b and target % g === 0.
steps: If target > a + b, return false: the jugs cannot hold that much.
Compute g = gcd(a, b) with Euclid: replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
pitfalls: Forgetting the capacity check. With a = 3, b = 5 every number is a multiple of gcd 1, but 9 still does not fit.
Thinking that a target smaller than both jugs is always possible. With jugs 4 and 6, the total 5 is never reached.
Running a search over all (x, y) states for jugs of a million litres. It works, but it is millions of states for a question a gcd answers.

solutions.title: Search over jug states
solutions.idea: Breadth-first search over (water in a, water in b), trying all six moves from each state, until some state has the target total.
solutions.time: O(a · b) in the worst case

solutions.title: Greatest common divisor
solutions.idea: Reachable totals are exactly the multiples of gcd(a, b) that fit in both jugs together.

followups: Return the shortest sequence of moves that reaches the target. Which of the two approaches can give you that?
There are three jugs instead of two. Does the gcd rule still hold, and does the capacity check change?
